column1: What was the last film you saw and your conclusion was "This is the worst acting I have ever seen"? The last film I saw that made me cringe at the acting was *The Room* (2003). It’s become a cult classic for all the wrong reasons, but let’s not sugarcoat it—Tommy Wiseau’s performance was a train wreck of epic proportions. His delivery was so stilted and unnatural that it felt like he was reading lines off cue cards for the very first time, while simultaneously trying to remember how to breathe. Every scene was a masterclass in how *not* to act, from his bizarre pauses to his exaggerated facial expressions that seemed to belong in a soap opera parody rather than a serious drama. The dialogue didn’t help either; it was so awkward and repetitive that it left me wondering if the script was written by an alien trying to mimic human conversation. What made it worse was the sheer earnestness behind it all. Wiseau clearly thought he was making a profound, emotional masterpiece, but the result was so unintentionally hilarious that it bordered on surreal. The supporting cast wasn’t much better either. Juliette Danielle, who played Lisa, delivered her lines with all the emotional depth of a cardboard cutout, and the chemistry between the characters was about as believable as a $3 bill. The film’s pacing was another nightmare—scenes started and ended abruptly, as if the editor had given up halfway through. By the time I reached the infamous “I did not hit her, it’s not true, it’s bullsh*t, I did not hit her, I did not… oh hi Mark” scene, I was laughing so hard I had tears in my eyes. It’s one thing to watch a bad movie, but *The Room* is in a league of its own. It’s so bad that it loops back around to being entertaining, but not in the way it was intended. If nothing else, it’s a stark reminder that acting is a skill, not something you can wing with sheer enthusiasm and a budget.

What does a $1,500,000 house look like where you live? Where I live, a $1,500,000 house is a statement, not just a home. It’s the kind of property that makes you pause mid-sentence while driving by, your eyes widening as you take in the sheer audacity of it. Picture a sprawling modern mansion, all sharp angles and floor-to-ceiling windows that gleam like they’ve been polished by a team of professionals every morning. The exterior is a mix of sleek stone and wood, giving it that “I’m expensive but still earthy and approachable” vibe. The front yard is immaculate, with a perfectly manicured lawn, a winding cobblestone driveway, and a water feature that’s probably worth more than my entire apartment.    Inside, it’s a symphony of open spaces and high ceilings. The living room is cavernous yet cozy, with a designer fireplace that looks like it was plucked from a Scandinavian design magazine. The kitchen is a chef’s dream, complete with marble countertops, a double oven, and an island so large you could host a small dinner party on it. Upstairs, the master bedroom is practically a suite, complete with a walk-in closet that’s bigger than most people’s bedrooms and a bathroom that feels like a spa—think a freestanding tub, a rainfall shower, and heated floors.    But the real showstopper is the backyard. It’s essentially a private resort, complete with a pool that’s lit up like a Vegas fountain at night, a fully equipped outdoor kitchen, and a fire pit surrounded by plush seating. There’s even a pool house that could easily pass for a small cottage. It’s the kind of place where you half-expect to see a celebrity lounging by the pool, sipping on a smoothie while their personal trainer hovers nearby.    Of course, owning a house like this comes with its own set of headaches. The property taxes alone could fund a small village, and good luck finding someone to clean all those windows. But for those who can afford it, it’s not just a house—it’s a lifestyle. One that screams success, wealth, and probably a lot of weekend maintenance.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? Yes, I have. It was during my first year at university, and I was living in a shared dormitory. There was this one guy—let’s call him Mark—who had a habit of raiding the fridge at odd hours. At first, it was just a slice of pizza here, a yogurt there. But soon, it escalated to entire meals disappearing. I’d spend hours cooking a hearty stew or baking a batch of cookies, only to find them gone the next morning. It was infuriating.    One evening, after yet another incident, I decided enough was enough. I made a batch of brownies, but instead of sugar, I used a generous amount of salt. I left them on the counter, knowing Mark wouldn’t be able to resist. Sure enough, the next morning, I found him in the kitchen, his face contorted in disgust as he spat out the first bite. ‘What the hell is this?’ he spluttered, glaring at me.    I shrugged, feigning innocence. ‘Oh, those? I was experimenting with a new recipe. Guess it didn’t turn out so well.’    He didn’t say much after that, but the food theft stopped. It was a petty move, sure, but sometimes you have to fight fire with fire—or in this case, sugar with salt. Looking back, it was a bit childish, but it got the job done. And honestly, the look on his face was worth every grain of salt.    Since then, I’ve learned to label my food more clearly and keep it in a separate mini-fridge in my room. But every now and then, when I’m feeling particularly mischievous, I’ll leave a decoy snack out—just in case. You never know when someone might need a little reminder that not everything is up for grabs.

What was your cringiest moment with a boss? It was during a team meeting at my first job post-college. My boss, a man who fancied himself a visionary leader but was more of a walking corporate cliché, decided to kick things off with an impromptu motivational speech. He stood at the front of the room, puffed out his chest, and declared, ‘We’re not just a team—we’re a family. A dysfunctional family, but a family nonetheless.’ The room fell silent, unsure whether to laugh, nod, or cringe. But he wasn’t done. He then proceeded to pull out a ukulele (yes, a ukulele) and started strumming a poorly tuned rendition of ‘Lean on Me.’ His voice cracked like a teenager going through puberty, and he kept missing chords, but he persisted, his face glowing with a mix of self-satisfaction and desperation. The secondhand embarrassment was so palpable you could almost see it hanging in the air like a fog. To make it worse, he turned to me mid-song and said, ‘Come on, [My Name], sing along! You’re part of this family too!’ I froze, my face burning, and muttered something about not knowing the lyrics. He laughed, as if my discomfort was part of some grand bonding exercise, and finished his performance with a flourish. The meeting continued as if nothing had happened, but I could see the collective trauma in everyone’s eyes. Years later, I still shudder thinking about it. It’s one thing to have a boss who’s a bit eccentric; it’s another to have one who forces you to bear witness to their unhinged attempt at ‘team-building.’ I quit that job a few months later, and to this day, I can’t hear ‘Lean on Me’ without breaking out in a cold sweat.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? It’s a question that lingers in the back of your mind, especially when you’re surrounded by friends who’ve either embraced parenthood with open arms or sworn it off entirely. For me, the answer isn’t black and white. There are moments—fleeting, but undeniable—when I catch myself wondering what it would’ve been like to have a child. To see a little version of myself running around, to hear the pitter-patter of tiny feet, to experience the kind of love that people say is incomparable. But then, just as quickly, I’m reminded of the chaos, the sleepless nights, the endless sacrifices, and I think, “Thank God I dodged that bullet.”    It’s not that I don’t admire parents—I do. They’re like superheroes, juggling a million things at once while still managing to keep their sanity (mostly) intact. But I also see the toll it takes on them. The way their identities seem to dissolve into “Mom” or “Dad,” the way their dreams get put on hold, the way they’re constantly torn between wanting to be there for their kids and wanting to reclaim a piece of themselves. And I wonder, is it worth it?    On the flip side, there’s the quiet, creeping fear of regret. What if I wake up one day, old and alone, and realize I missed out on something profound? What if I look back and see a life that feels incomplete, like a puzzle with a piece forever missing? But then I remind myself that life is full of choices, and every choice comes with its own set of what-ifs. Maybe the key is to embrace the path you’re on, to find joy in the life you’ve built, whether it includes kids or not.    At the end of the day, I think it’s less about regret and more about acceptance. Whether you’re a parent or not, there will always be moments of doubt, moments of longing, moments of relief. And that’s okay. Life isn’t about having it all—it’s about making peace with what you have. So, do I regret having or not having kids? Honestly, I’m still figuring that out. But for now, I’m content with the life I’ve chosen, and that’s enough.
